title: Automating review requests without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Review requests after the work arrives
excerpt: Ask for a review once, after delivery, and only if nothing is still wrong. Skip the drip, the bribe, and the request in the middle of a complaint.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree. A review request should wait until the work is as settled as that room.
caption: A settled room. The ask waits until the work is finished. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is it reasonable to ask for a review?
faqs.answer: After delivery is real: the shipment has arrived and had a moment to be opened, or the project milestone a person confirmed is in their hands. Checkout is too early. If a complaint, return, or dispute is open, do not ask.

faqs.question: How many times should you ask?
faqs.answer: Once, with one link, in a template a person approved. A second note is a human exception, not a drip. Do not attach a coupon or a script for them to paste. People who wanted to review will have used the first link.

faqs.question: Should a studio automate a client reference request?
faqs.answer: An internal reminder that the project shipped can be automatic. The note asking a client to be a reference should come from the person who did the work, at a moment that is not the invoice. A template after a tense project is how you lose the reference.

markdown:
Review request automation should ask for a review only after the customer has the work, only once, and only if nothing is still wrong. The ask is a small favor. A sequence that nags, bribes, or asks in the middle of a problem will spend the relationship to collect a star.

Automate the handoff around that moment of delivery. The machine may notice that the work was delivered, check that no complaint is open, and draft the ask from a template. Keep a person on anything the customer will see until the template has earned trust, on anything that offers money or a gift, and on anything you cannot undo, such as a public reply or a request sent to someone who is still waiting for a fix. Measure minutes of remembering to ask against minutes of review, and count complaints about the ask itself.

## Wait until delivery is real

Checkout is not delivery. A request that leaves the moment they pay is a request about a hope. For a physical good, delivery means the carrier's handoff or, better, a short delay after that so the object has been opened. For a project, delivery means they have the launch, the files, or the milestone you named, and a person has confirmed it is the thing you said you would send. For a service visit, it means the visit happened, not that it was booked.

Write the trigger in a sentence your team agrees with. "Three days after the shipment is marked delivered, if no support thread is open, draft the ask." If you cannot name a reliable delivered state, do not automate the ask. A person can send a few notes a week. A machine that guesses "they must have it by now" will ask people who are staring at an empty doorstep.

The delay is part of the design. Too soon and you are interrupting unboxing with homework. Too late and they have moved on, and the review will be vague or absent. Pick a delay you would tolerate as a customer, and keep it stable so you can tell whether the ask is welcome.

Suppress the draft when there is an open complaint, a return, a refund in progress, or a project thread that is still arguing about scope. Asking for praise while you owe them a fix is the fastest way to earn a detailed public criticism. The workflow can read a flag a person maintains: "do not ask." It should not decide from sentiment that the customer "seems fine."

## One ask, in words you can say aloud

The template is short. It names the work they received, asks once, and gives a single link to the place you actually want the review. It thanks them without flattery. It does not include a star rating they must hit, a script to paste, or a warning that you will keep writing.

One ask is the sequence. A second note is a person deciding that this customer is an exception, not a drip campaign with three subject lines. People who wanted to review will have used the first link. People who did not will experience the second as debt. You are running a studio or a shop, not a ratings acquisition desk.

Do not offer a coupon, a gift, or a discount in exchange for the review inside this workflow. Incentives change what the review means, and they are the kind of promise that is awkward to undo if the tool offers them to the wrong buyer or to every buyer. If you ever run a lawful, disclosed program like that, a person designs it on purpose. It does not ride along in a template because a tool suggested "boost response."

Do not ask them to review on five sites. One place. If they already left a review, suppress. Asking again reads as if you did not notice, which is a small insult after they did you the favor.

Google's guide to [creating helpful, reliable people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is aimed at pages, and it still governs this ask. A review you solicit should be something a real customer can write from experience. People-first means you are not manufacturing lines for a search result or a badge. Do not send talking points that turn their review into your copy. If the review is useful, it will be in their words, including the mild ones.

## What a person still checks

Until the trigger has been right for a long stretch, a person releases the draft. The check is mechanical.

- The delivered state is true for this order or this milestone.
- No support, return, or dispute flag is set.
- The name and the item match. A review request for the wrong product is a confession that you are not paying attention.
- The link is the review link, not a tracking link and not a reorder link dressed up as a favor.

If the template ever includes a sentence that is not from the approved text, it becomes a full read again. A model that adds "we hope you loved it" has assumed the outcome. Some of them did not love it, and they have not told you yet. Neutral wording survives that case. "If you have a minute, a review helps other people decide" survives it. "Tell everyone how amazing your photoshoot was" does not.

A public reply to a review, later, is a separate act. The workflow that asked does not also answer the review in public. Public replies are easy to get wrong, and they are permanent in a way a private thank-you is not. A person writes them, and only when a reply is useful.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover the shops and the product work people are later asked to judge, plus the small automations around delivery. The ask belongs after that work is real, in one sentence, from a sender the customer recognizes.

## Minutes saved against minutes of review

Time the old habit. How many deliveries left without an ask because nobody remembered, and how long did it take when someone did remember? Include finding the right link and checking they were not already unhappy. That check is the part worth keeping.

Time the new release. If it is a glance at flags and a send, you have saved the remembering. If every draft needs a rewrite, the template is doing too much. Cut it until the glance is enough.

Count two signals for a month. Complaints about being asked, and reviews that mention the request as pressure. A few people will always dislike being asked. A pattern means the timing or the second nudge is wrong. Also count asks sent to people with open problems. That number should be zero. It is the relationship metric. The count of reviews collected is not, on its own, the success of the automation.

If the review rate is low and the complaints are low, you may still leave the system in place. A quiet, accurate ask is allowed to convert modestly. Do not "optimize" it into urgency. The subject line does not need to sound like a deadline.

## When they reply to the ask

Some people will write back instead of clicking the link. Treat that reply as mail from a customer, not as a failed conversion. If they describe a problem, a person answers the problem and the review link does not get sent again. If they say something kind and do not want to post it, thank them and stop. Do not paste their private note into a public review widget. That is a disclosure they did not offer.

If they ask how the review will be used, the answer is the plain one: it may appear on the site or on the platform you linked, under their name if that platform shows names. A person can say that. The template should not have promised anonymity if the platform does not provide it, and it should not have promised a feature on your homepage. You can decide later, as an editor, to quote a line with permission. The automation does not harvest quotes.

A reply that is abusive or confused still gets a person's judgment. Mute the automation for that order so a follow-up cannot fire, and answer or close the thread the way you would any other customer note. The ask is over once they have spoken, even if they never left a star.

## Who sends it, and who never receives it

Send from a named person or from the brand they bought from, consistently. A stranger's address, or a new tool's domain, looks like a phish, especially when it contains a link. Use the same identity you used for the receipt.

Never send to a customer who opted out of mail, who is a wholesale buyer with a different agreement, or who received a comp you would not ask to review. Never send to your own team as a test against the live list. The suppression list is part of the workflow, and a person owns additions to it.

For a client project rather than a shop order, think harder before you automate at all. A review of a studio engagement is a reference. It deserves a personal note from the person who did the work, at a moment that is not the invoice. The workflow can remind you internally that the project shipped and a reference might be appropriate. The note itself stays handwritten. Automating that favor is how a client who just finished a tense project receives a template, and declines to be a reference at all.

Keep the trigger, the delay, and the suppression rules written next to the template. When you add a new product line, decide the delay again. A candle and a custom sofa do not share a "three days later." The sofa may not be in the room for weeks. Ask when it is in the room.

This series has been about keeping a person on the message. The next problem is the shop itself, and the object in it. [An online shop for a ceramics studio](/blog/an-online-shop-for-a-ceramics-studio) is the piece to read when the thing you sell has to be understood in the hand before anyone should be asked to pay, or to review it.
